opus-5.5.text:
I think the two matter in different ways, but if I had to rank them, I'd say the framework and the underlying model capability come first, and the front-end is what determines whether that capability actually reaches people.

From the model side, what we care about is whether the agent can really complete a task end to end: can it plan, call tools reliably, recover when something goes wrong, keep context over a long horizon. A lot of that is shaped by the framework, how you structure the loop, what tools you expose, how you manage memory and feedback. If the framework is poorly designed, even a strong model looks weak, because it's being asked to do things in an awkward way. And in practice, the framework and the model co-evolve. When we train for agentic abilities, we're implicitly training against some kind of environment and interface, so the framework almost becomes part of the model's "body."

But I don't want to underestimate the front-end. The interface defines what the user expects, how they express intent, and how much they trust the system. A chat box invites short questions. A workspace where the agent can show its plan, its intermediate steps, and let you intervene invites much more ambitious tasks. So the UI actually shapes the distribution of tasks people bring, which in turn shapes what data you get and what you optimize for next. That loop is very important.

So my view is: in the early stage, capability and framework are the bottleneck. You can't design a great experience around something that doesn't work. But once the core ability crosses a certain threshold, the product form and interaction design become the differentiator, because many teams will have similarly capable models, and the question becomes who finds the right way to let people actually use it. Ideally you don't separate the two too much; the people building the model should be thinking about how it will be used, and the people designing the interface should understand what the model can and can't do.

r001.rationale: The response describes how the framework shapes agent behavior and how the UI shapes user interaction, but does not characterize the framework as an intermediary between people and models.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that a substantial framework can coexist with a very thin front-end; it instead discusses a workspace UI with plans, intermediate steps, and user intervention.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think of it as a ranking, honestly. People love to ask "which matters more," and my answer is that they're solving different problems and the mistake is treating one as downstream of the other.

The agent framework is where the capability actually lives. How does the model decompose a task, how does it decide when to call a tool, how does it recover when a step fails, how does it manage context over a long horizon. If you get that wrong, no interface saves you. A beautiful chat window on top of an agent that loops or hallucinates a file path is just a nicer way to be disappointed.

But here's what I think people underestimate about the front end. The interface isn't decoration on top of the agent. It's part of the agent's feedback loop. The user is a sensor. When they can see what the agent is doing, interrupt it, correct a plan before it executes, that information flows back into the system. A good interface makes the human a better collaborator, and that makes the overall system more capable than the model alone. So in a real sense, interface design is agent design.

Where I'd put the asymmetry is in the order of operations. Early on, when the model isn't reliable yet, you need a lot of interface. Visibility, confirmation steps, undo. As the underlying capability improves, you can take scaffolding away. So the framework determines the ceiling, and the interface determines how much of that ceiling a normal person can actually reach today.

The teams that go wrong usually do one of two things. Either they pour everything into the model and ship something only researchers can operate, or they build a gorgeous product around a model that can't yet do what the product promises. I'd rather be slightly ugly and genuinely capable, and then let the interface catch up fast, because iterating on UI is much cheaper than iterating on reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response describes the framework’s capabilities and the interface’s feedback loop, but does not characterize the framework as an intermediary between people and models.

r002.rationale: It discusses reducing interface scaffolding as capability improves, but does not state that a substantial framework can coexist with a very thin front-end UI.

astra-6.text:
I think the agent framework is more fundamental, but the front end is what makes that capability useful to people. The framework determines whether the agent can understand a task, use tools, and carry it through reliably. A polished interface can’t compensate for an agent that doesn’t get the work done.

But I wouldn’t treat the interface as just a layer of decoration. With an agent, you need to communicate intent, see enough of what it’s doing to trust it, and intervene when it goes in the wrong direction. Those are interaction problems as much as model or framework problems.

So I’d prioritize the framework early, while designing the interface around the actual workflow. The two need to evolve together: better capabilities create new ways to interact, and real user interactions reveal what the framework is missing.

r001.rationale: The response says the framework determines what the agent can do, but does not characterize it as an intermediary between people and models.

r002.rationale: It prioritizes the framework while saying the framework and interface should evolve together; it does not state that a substantial framework can coexist with a very thin UI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the agent framework and the front-end interface solve two different but closely connected problems. The framework determines what the agent can actually do: how it uses tools, manages context, and completes a task reliably. The interface determines whether users can understand those capabilities and work with them effectively.

For agents, the interface is especially important because the interaction goes beyond asking a question and receiving an answer. Users need to see what the agent is doing, provide input when necessary, and correct its direction. A powerful framework can still feel unusable if that interaction is poorly designed.

So I wouldn’t assign a fixed percentage of importance to either one. I would start with the user’s task and develop them together. The framework makes the capability possible, and the interface makes it useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes what the framework enables, but does not characterize it as an intermediary between people and models.

r002.rationale: It discusses the framework and interface as connected, but does not state that a substantial framework can coexist with a very thin front-end UI.
